column1: # DELIBERATELY UNBOUND SYMBOLS -- the checked-in half of the bidirectional control in
# android/gate/boundverbledger_test.go.
# WHY IT EXISTS. A gomobile facade makes "exists" and "is used" independent BY CONSTRUCTION:
# the Go side compiles and tests green with no caller at all, because its callers are in a
# language the Go toolchain never sees. Six separate defects shipped that way in Phase B, each
# found later than the last, every one of them unit-tested and traced in a coverage artifact.
# The generalisable control is bidirectional: every bound verb is either CALLED from production
# Kotlin or LISTED here with a reason. A new verb is then uncallable-by-default loudly rather
# than silently.
# THIS IS NOT A LIST OF THINGS THAT DO NOT MATTER. Every App row below is traced to a screen
# element in mobile/screen_coverage.tsv, so each one is product surface somebody eventually
# needs; what each row records is the screen that does not exist yet on the minimal S18/S19
# surface. Two rows (IsRunning, Resize) are the exception and say so.
# WHAT THE CHECK CANNOT SEE, so this file is not read as a complete inventory of unreachable
# facade surface:
#   App.InstallWakeKey and App.InstallContentKey read as CALLED and are not. They are called
#   through the `CoreKeyCustody` interface (keys/Custody.kt), whose only implementation in the
#   repository is the test fixture `RecordingCore`. No production class implements it, so
#   `KeyCustodySession` -- the class holding ADR-007 B8's single deliberate Java -> Go key
#   crossing -- has no production caller either. Establishing that needs a type checker; the
#   check matches names. It is recorded here rather than left to be discovered a seventh time.
#   The INSTALL half is superseded rather than merely unwired (ADR-007 B35): PB-KEY-10 moved
#   epoch-key delivery entirely into Go, so the Kotlin side has no source for those bytes and a
#   wired adapter would have thrown on its first call. App.PurgeKeys is no longer in this
#   paragraph: it is called from `PhoneRuntime.lockContent`, reached from
#   `dev.swarm.phone.runtime.ContentLock` on every InvalidationEvent, and its recovery half
#   App.UnlockContent from `PhoneRuntime.unlockContent` -- both by direct call on the bound App,
#   which the name-matching check does see.
# THE LEDGER COVERS EVERY BOUND RECEIVER, not just `App`. It was hardcoded to the `App`
# receiver until 2026-07-26, and four bound methods lived in the blind spot that left --
# SessionList.Stale, JournalPage.Stale, JournalPage.NextCursor and UndeliveredList.Dropped, each
# a fact the facade goes to the trouble of carrying and the adapter dropped on the floor. The
# first three are now read by FacadeBridge; the rows below are what is left.
# Columns: symbol <TAB> reason
# Symbols are namespaced: App.<Verb> and <Handle>.<Method> for a bound facade method,
# FacadeBridge.<method> for the one adapter between the screen models and the facade.
#symbol
App.ClearUndeliveredInputs
column2: PB-INPUT-1's undelivered-input ledger has no screen. The acknowledgement half cannot be wired before the list it acknowledges, and neither exists on the minimal surface. Pairs with App.UndeliveredInputs.

column1: App.UndeliveredInputs
column2: PB-INPUT-1's "and that the UX state appears": input is live-only, so nothing is ever retried and the user must be TOLD what did not reach the machine. The surface has a keyboard and no place to show the backlog. A real product gap, not a retired verb.

column1: App.Paste
column2: PB-INPUT-6's atomic paste -- a clipboard paste or an IME COMMIT as ONE event rather than a keystroke stream. The keyboard is an EditText plus Send line, which is the coalesced keystroke path; nothing on the surface offers a paste action.

column1: App.Resize
column2: Nothing on this surface can change the terminal geometry, and after ADR-009-structured-chat-interaction there is no geometry to change: the phone draws a structured transcript and no grid, so there are no cols/rows a user could choose and no viewport for a resize to describe. It was already unbound while the peek was a monospace TextView printing the daemon-rendered grid byte for byte; what changed is that the screen it was waiting for is now one the design has retired rather than one nobody has built.

column1: App.IsRunning
column2: Legitimately unbound: it is a redundant read. App.Start is idempotent and PhoneSurface.converge decides from LifecycleConvergence plus App.StateSummary, so asking whether the app is running would be a second source for a fact the plan already settles.

column1: App.PendingOpCount
column2: PB-SYNC-2's aggregate. This surface claims outcomes BY OPERATION ID (FacadeBridge.launchOutcome, used by SettingsSurface), which is the requirement's own discipline; a count is for a screen that shows in-flight work, and there is none.

column1: App.Presence
column2: PB-APP-5's machine presence, and the one row here that is a DECISION rather than a missing screen. It is a blocking relay round-trip, and this surface's render() is driven by an event stream -- so calling it per redraw would issue a relay RPC per journal record. THE ANSWER LANDED, AND IT IS NOT THIS VERB (bead agents-tracker-xtj): the cadence now lives in Go, on the relay goroutine, and a screen reads App.MachinePresence, which is a cached O(1) read. This verb stays exported and stays unbound for one reason -- PB-NET-7's connection-leak test uses it as its real request/reply exchange, to retire a USED connection rather than an idle one, so turning it into the cached read would have left that test green and testing nothing. Kotlin must never call it.

column1: App.MachinePresence
column2: The cached presence reading the Machines pane exists to render, and unbound only until the Android lane frees (bead agents-tracker-xtj). The Go half landed first on purpose: the AAR is rebuilt and the Kotlin wired in one pass, and adding the verb now means the screen is written against a facade that already answers instead of against a literal. It is the verb a render may call -- App.Presence is not.

column1: App.PairedDeviceName
column2: The paired device's name for the Machines pane, unbound until the Android lane frees (bead agents-tracker-xtj). It returns the constant this side owns and sends at enrolment, because the wire never returns it: a screen that typed the string would be rendering a Go constant as though the machine had said it, which is ADR-007 B135's defect class and the reason this is a verb rather than a Kotlin literal.

column1: App.Peek
column2: The daemon-rendered terminal grid, and the FIRST row here that is a retired screen rather than a missing one. FacadeBridge.terminalPeek read it on every draw until docs/adr/ADR-009-structured-chat-interaction.md (1) left "no terminal emulation and no raw grid anywhere in the app" and (3) dated the well's deletion to slice I1's exit. The verb is deliberately NOT deleted: (2) narrows the machine-side renderer's role without withdrawing it -- internal/daemon/terminalrender.go is still the sanitization choke point, TerminalSnapshot and terminal_watch stay on the wire unchanged, and the generic fallback adapter and the prompt-card fallback are both machine-side consumers of it. What is gone is a phone surface RENDERING a grid to a human. Pairs with App.TerminalWatch: with no watch issued, the cache this reads is never filled.

column1: App.TerminalWatch
column2: The request that makes the machine push terminal frames for one session. ADR-009 (2) is explicit that "no phone surface issues a watch", and (7) is why it matters rather than being tidiness: the machine-to-phone budget is <= 8 appends/s across journal AND terminal combined for one target, and with no snapshot frames appended the transcript inherits the whole of what the peek used to spend. Unbound as a DECISION, like App.Presence's row, and not as a screen nobody has built yet -- Kotlin must not call it again without amending that ADR. Pairs with App.TerminalUnwatch and App.Peek.

column1: App.TerminalUnwatch
column2: The close half of App.TerminalWatch, unbound with it and for one reason only: there is nothing left to close. It existed so the peek plane did not leak per-session server render work for every session a user ever looked at; a phone that opens no watch leaks none. It stays exported because the verb pairs with a watch this app may never issue but the protocol still defines.

column1: App.ReleaseControl
column2: PB-INPUT-3's take_control_end. The surface can TAKE a lease and cannot give one back, so a lease is held until the machine expires it. SessionLease.showsRelease is the model that would drive the control -- it was TerminalPeek.showsRelease until the terminal well's deletion (ADR-009 (3)) left the three lease properties behind as their own model. A real product gap.

column1: App.Resync
column2: PB-SYNC-1's per-stream repair, and THE REASON ON THIS ROW CHANGED when the screen it was waiting for landed. It used to read "the stale/repairing screen ... does not exist", which is now false: LinkPanel draws all four channels on the Machines destination. What is still missing is the CONTROL, and it is a screen decision rather than a wiring one -- the verb is rate-bounded per section 6.0 (<= 1 per stream per 5 s, <= 12 per 5 min) and refuses with ErrClassRateLimited, so a button needs a place to render that refusal and a rule for what it says while a repair it already asked for is in flight. Consequence, stated rather than left to be inferred: nothing sets resyncAsked, so App.ResyncPending is always false and StreamBadge.RESYNCING is unreachable in production. Tracked as agents-tracker-upbo.

column1: App.KillSwitchEngaged
column2: PB-APP-5/PB-SEC-6, READ ONLY by design -- the phone may never SET the switch. It exists so a CodeKillSwitch refusal is legible, and legibility needs a place to put it: the surface routes refusals through PB-APP-9's taxonomy and has no machine-status pane.

column1: FacadeBridge.sessionRow
column2: One row BY ID, for a session detail screen (inventory C2). S24's triage inbox renders the whole roster through TriageInbox and a tapped row carries its own id, so the surface still never looks a session up by id -- it already has the row. What would need this is a screen that opens ON one session and reads it fresh; there is none. Carries App.Session with it.

column1: UndeliveredList.Dropped
column2: PB-INPUT-1's overflow count: how many undelivered records were discarded because the ledger itself is bounded. It cannot be wired before the list it counts, and App.UndeliveredInputs has no screen (see its own row) -- a count with no list beside it is a number the user cannot act on. Pairs with App.UndeliveredInputs and App.ClearUndeliveredInputs.

column1: Pairing.DeadlineMillis
column2: PB-PAIR-4's countdown, and the one row here that is a DECISION rather than a missing screen. The 60 s rendezvous TTL is the RELAY's and the phone's own deadline is derived from it, so a ticking display would be the phone asserting an expiry only the relay can enforce -- and PairingStep.RENDEZVOUS_TIMEOUT already tells the user the same thing at the moment it becomes true, with a next step attached.
